questions.stem: In VCE Psychology, resilience is defined as:
options: the absence of any symptoms of a mental health concern
the ability to avoid all situations that might cause stress
a consistently high level of functioning in daily tasks
the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty
questions.explanation: Resilience is the ability to cope with and manage change and uncertainty, recovering after difficulties. A resilient person still experiences stress; avoiding stressors is not what resilience means.

questions.stem: When considering mental wellbeing, 'levels of functioning' refers to:
options: how well a person can independently complete everyday tasks, such as study, work and self-care
the number of protective factors in a person's life across biological, psychological and social areas
the strength of a person's physiological stress response when they are faced with a stressor
the stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome that a person has reached during chronic stress
questions.explanation: Levels of functioning describe a person's ability to carry out the tasks of daily life independently and effectively. High functioning is one sign of good mental wellbeing; a drop in functioning can signal a decline.

questions.stem: Which example best illustrates a high level of resilience?
options: After losing her part-time job, Lena adjusts her budget, applies for new jobs and is back to her usual mood within weeks
After losing her part-time job, Lena refuses to think about it for months and avoids friends who ask how she is going
After losing her part-time job, Lena's mood drops and stays low for most of the year, affecting her school results
Lena has never lost a job or faced any other kind of setback, so she has never had to adapt to change or uncertainty at all
questions.explanation: Resilience is shown by adapting to change and recovering, as Lena does by problem-solving and returning to her usual mood. Never facing a setback says nothing about how well she would cope with one.

questions.stem: Mental wellbeing is described as a continuum because:
options: once a person has developed a mental disorder, their level of wellbeing can no longer change
mental wellbeing is influenced only by internal factors, such as genetics, and not by external ones
a person's wellbeing can shift along a range from mentally healthy to mental disorder over time
a person is either mentally healthy or has a mental disorder, with no states in between the two
questions.explanation: The continuum view sees wellbeing as a range that a person moves along as internal and external factors interact, so it fluctuates over time. Treating it as two fixed categories ignores the many states between being mentally healthy and having a disorder.

questions.stem: Which is an external factor that can influence a person's mental wellbeing?
options: A habit of persistent negative thinking
Low levels of GABA in the brain
The breakdown of a close friendship
A genetic vulnerability to anxiety
questions.explanation: External factors come from outside the person, such as relationships, events and environment. Genetics, thinking patterns and neurotransmitter levels are internal factors.

questions.stem: How does anxiety typically differ from stress?
options: Anxiety is always a diagnosable mental disorder, whereas stress is a normal response that does not affect a person's wellbeing
Anxiety involves only physiological responses, whereas stress involves only psychological responses such as worry
Anxiety is worry about a possible future threat and can persist without a clear stressor; stress is a response to an identified stressor
Stress is worry about a possible future threat and can persist without a clear stressor; anxiety is a response to an identified stressor
questions.explanation: Stress is a response to a specific stressor, while anxiety is a state of apprehension, often about something uncertain in the future, that can continue after a stressor has passed. Anxiety is not always a disorder, and both involve psychological and physiological responses.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes a specific phobia from ordinary fear?
options: The fear is mild and brief, and the person can easily carry on with what they were doing
The fear is about a vague future event rather than a particular object or situation
The fear is intense and out of proportion to the danger, and avoidance disrupts daily life
The fear is felt in response to a real and immediate threat to the person's physical safety
questions.explanation: A specific phobia is an anxiety disorder involving intense, irrational fear of a particular object or situation, leading to avoidance that interferes with functioning. Fear of a real, immediate threat is an adaptive response, and vague worry about the future is more typical of anxiety.

questions.stem: Which comparison of stress, anxiety and specific phobia on the mental wellbeing continuum is most accurate?
options: Anxiety is experienced only by people who have a diagnosed mental disorder such as phobia
Specific phobia typically disrupts functioning more persistently than everyday stress or anxiety
Everyday stress typically causes more persistent disruption to functioning than a specific phobia
Stress, anxiety and phobia are the same state, as all three are short responses to one stressor
questions.explanation: Everyday stress and anxiety are common, often temporary and usually manageable, whereas a specific phobia is a mental disorder that persists and significantly affects functioning. Mentally healthy people also experience anxiety at times.

questions.stem: Which biological factor can contribute to the development of a specific phobia?
options: Excess GABA, which over-inhibits neurons in the fear pathways
Damage to the cerebellum, which removes procedural memories
A lack of melatonin, which is secreted by the pineal gland
GABA dysfunction, which reduces inhibition of the fear response
questions.explanation: GABA dysfunction means neurons involved in the fear response are not inhibited enough, so the response is triggered too easily. Excess GABA would reduce, not increase, anxious arousal.

questions.stem: How does GABA dysfunction contribute to phobic anxiety?
options: Too little GABA activity leaves neurons in fear pathways under-inhibited, so the stress response fires more readily
Too much GABA activity over-excites neurons in fear pathways, so the stress response fires more readily
GABA is the main excitatory neurotransmitter, so lower levels make a person feel calmer and less anxious
GABA dysfunction blocks all new memory formation, so the person cannot remember that the stimulus is actually harmless
questions.explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. If it is not working effectively, neural activity in fear pathways is not dampened, making the sympathetic stress response more likely. GABA inhibits rather than excites neurons.

questions.stem: How can long-term potentiation contribute to the development of a specific phobia?
options: Long-term potentiation weakens the pathways that link the stimulus with fear, so the phobia forms when it stops occurring
Long-term potentiation releases GABA at fear synapses, and that GABA is what triggers the phobic fear response
Long-term potentiation prunes connections between the amygdala and hippocampus, so fear memories cannot be updated
Repeated activation of the pathway linking the stimulus with fear strengthens it, so the fear response becomes more automatic
questions.explanation: Each time the phobic stimulus and fear are activated together, the synaptic connections between them are strengthened through long-term potentiation. This makes the fear response faster and harder to change. LTP strengthens rather than weakens connections.

questions.stem: Behavioural models propose that a specific phobia is:
options: precipitated by catastrophic thinking and perpetuated by memory bias
precipitated by classical conditioning and perpetuated by operant conditioning
precipitated by operant conditioning and perpetuated by classical conditioning
precipitated by observational learning and perpetuated by GABA dysfunction
questions.explanation: Classical conditioning explains how a phobia begins, through an association between a stimulus and fear. Operant conditioning explains why it continues, as avoidance is negatively reinforced. Catastrophic thinking and memory bias are cognitive biases, not behavioural models.

questions.stem: After being stuck in a lift during a blackout, Erin now panics whenever she enters a lift. In classical conditioning terms, the lift is the:
options: conditioned stimulus
unconditioned stimulus
conditioned response
unconditioned response
questions.explanation: The lift was a neutral stimulus that became associated with the frightening experience of being trapped, so it now triggers fear on its own as a conditioned stimulus. Being trapped in the dark was the unconditioned stimulus.

questions.stem: Erin now always takes the stairs instead of the lift, and her anxiety drops each time she does. How does this perpetuate her phobia?
options: Avoiding the lift removes her anxiety, so avoidance is negatively reinforced and she never learns lifts are safe
Taking the stairs is a form of positive punishment, so each time she does it her fear of lifts becomes even stronger
Avoiding the lift is positively reinforced by the exercise she gets, which reduces her fear of lifts
Taking the stairs extinguishes the conditioned response, so her fear of lifts slowly returns
questions.explanation: Avoidance removes an unpleasant feeling, anxiety, so the avoidance behaviour is negatively reinforced and becomes more likely. Because she never rides a lift, she has no chance to learn that lifts are safe. Negative reinforcement removes something unpleasant; it is not punishment.

questions.stem: Catastrophic thinking is a cognitive bias in which a person:
options: expects the worst possible outcome of a situation
remembers past events as less threatening than they were
seeks out information that disproves their beliefs
avoids the feared stimulus to reduce their anxiety
questions.explanation: Catastrophic thinking involves predicting or exaggerating the worst possible outcome. Avoidance is a behaviour, not a cognitive bias.

questions.stem: Jaya, who fears dogs, recalls a dog that once barked at her as huge and about to attack, though others who were there say it was small and on a lead. This is an example of:
options: a social trigger
memory bias
catastrophic thinking
negative reinforcement
questions.explanation: Jaya's recall of a past event has been distorted to fit her fear, which is memory bias. Catastrophic thinking is about expecting the worst outcome in a present or future situation, not misremembering a past one.

questions.stem: Which thought is an example of catastrophic thinking in a person with a fear of flying?
options: 'People will think I'm weak if I see a psychologist about my fear.'
'If there's any turbulence, the plane will crash and I'll die.'
'My last flight was terrifying, even though others say it was smooth.'
'I'll catch the train instead so that I don't have to feel anxious.'
questions.explanation: Assuming turbulence will end in disaster is catastrophic thinking, as it jumps to the worst possible outcome. Remembering a smooth flight as terrifying is memory bias, and catching the train is avoidance.

questions.stem: How can stigma around seeking treatment contribute to a specific phobia?
options: Stigma is the unconditioned stimulus that first produces the fear in classical conditioning
Stigma leads the person to appraise the phobic stimulus as irrelevant, so they avoid it
Fear of being judged may stop a person seeking help, so the phobia continues untreated
Stigma raises GABA levels in the brain, which strengthens the conditioned fear response
questions.explanation: Stigma is a social factor: if a person expects to be judged as weak or strange, they may avoid seeking treatment, so the phobia is maintained. Stigma does not act on GABA or serve as the original conditioning event.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a specific environmental trigger for a phobia of dogs?
options: Expecting every dog to be dangerous
Inheriting a tendency towards anxiety
Being bitten by a dog at a local park
Low levels of GABA activity in the brain
questions.explanation: A specific environmental trigger is an event in the person's environment, such as a frightening encounter with the stimulus. Low GABA and inherited tendencies are biological factors, and expecting danger is a cognitive bias.

questions.stem: Ali has a spider phobia. Which correctly classifies these factors in a biopsychosocial approach: low GABA activity; always avoiding the garden; being bitten by a spider as a child?
options: Biological; social; psychological
Psychological; biological; social
Social; psychological; biological
Biological; psychological; social
questions.explanation: GABA dysfunction is biological. Avoidance, which is perpetuated by operant conditioning, is a psychological factor. A specific environmental trigger, such as the childhood bite, is a social factor in the study design's approach.

questions.stem: Which statement about the relative influences of factors in the development of specific phobia is most accurate?
options: A phobia always develops from a single factor, and this factor is the same for everyone with phobia
Social factors only influence how a phobia is treated and never how the phobia first developed
Biological, psychological and social factors interact, and their relative influence differs between people
Biological factors alone determine whether a phobia develops, so psychological and social factors add nothing
questions.explanation: A biopsychosocial approach holds that phobias result from interacting factors, and the balance of factors varies from person to person. No single factor explains every case.

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines are described as GABA agonists because they:
options: enhance the inhibitory effect of GABA at its receptor sites
block GABA receptor sites to stop GABA from having an effect
replace glutamate as the main excitatory neurotransmitter
increase the release of cortisol to calm the stress response
questions.explanation: An agonist mimics or enhances a neurotransmitter's effect. Benzodiazepines bind to GABA receptors and increase GABA's inhibitory effect, reducing the physiological symptoms of anxiety. Blocking GABA receptors would be the action of an antagonist.

questions.stem: What is a limitation of using benzodiazepines to manage specific phobia?
options: They permanently remove all conditioned fear, so the person also loses useful fears of real danger
They reduce anxiety symptoms but do not address the learned fear, and can lead to dependence
They raise physiological arousal before exposure, so the person's anxiety becomes even stronger
They take many months to have any effect, so they cannot help with phobic anxiety in the moment
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines are short-acting and calm the physiological response, but the phobia's learned and cognitive causes remain, and regular use risks dependence. They act quickly, which is why they are used for short-term management.

questions.stem: Breathing retraining helps a person manage phobic anxiety by:
options: replacing anxious, unrealistic thoughts about the phobic stimulus with more realistic ones
exposing the person to the phobic stimulus in small steps while they remain relaxed
teaching slow, controlled breathing that reduces sympathetic arousal and hyperventilation
increasing the breathing rate so the body takes in more oxygen to deal with the threat
questions.explanation: Breathing retraining is a biological intervention that counters the rapid, shallow breathing of the stress response, reducing physiological arousal. Challenging thoughts is part of CBT, and graded exposure is systematic desensitisation.

questions.stem: In systematic desensitisation, the fear response to the phobic stimulus is replaced with:
options: an avoidance response that is negatively reinforced over time
an unconditioned response to an entirely different stimulus
a relaxation response, which cannot occur at the same time as fear
a stronger fear response that eventually exhausts the person
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation uses classical conditioning to associate the phobic stimulus with relaxation, a response incompatible with fear. Strengthening avoidance would maintain the phobia rather than treat it.

questions.stem: Which feature is essential to systematic desensitisation?
options: Immediate exposure to the most feared item on the hierarchy, continuing until the anxiety subsides
Challenging irrational thoughts about the stimulus without ever exposing the person to the stimulus
Taking a benzodiazepine before each session so that the person feels no anxiety during exposure
Gradual exposure, moving up the fear hierarchy only when the person is relaxed at the current step
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation works through a fear hierarchy, from least to most feared, pairing each step with relaxation before moving on. Immediate exposure to the most feared item is a different technique, flooding.

questions.stem: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) treats specific phobia by:
options: educating family members about the phobia without involving the person who has it
helping the person identify and challenge unrealistic thoughts and change avoidance behaviours
prescribing short-acting GABA agonists to reduce the physiological symptoms of phobic anxiety
teaching slow, controlled breathing to reduce hyperventilation during a phobic reaction
questions.explanation: CBT targets both cognitions and behaviours: it challenges catastrophic or biased thoughts and replaces avoidance with more adaptive behaviour. Medication and breathing retraining are biological interventions.

questions.stem: A CBT therapist asks Ali, 'What evidence is there that this spider will hurt you?' The therapist is most directly targeting:
options: negative reinforcement, by removing the feared spider
stigma, by educating Ali's family about his phobia
catastrophic thinking, by challenging an unrealistic belief
GABA dysfunction, by changing neurotransmitter activity
questions.explanation: Asking for evidence is a cognitive technique that challenges an unrealistic expectation of harm, which is catastrophic thinking. It does not act directly on neurotransmitters, and it does not remove the stimulus.

questions.stem: Which intervention for specific phobia is classed as psychological in a biopsychosocial approach?
options: Breathing retraining
Psychoeducation for families
Systematic desensitisation
Benzodiazepine medication
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitisation, like CBT, is a psychotherapeutic treatment. In the study design, benzodiazepines and breathing retraining are biological interventions, and psychoeducation for families is social.

questions.stem: Psychoeducation for the families and supporters of a person with a phobia emphasises:
options: protecting the person from ever encountering the phobic stimulus in their daily life
reassuring the person that their fears are justified so they feel understood
encouraging the person to take benzodiazepines whenever they feel anxious
challenging the person's unrealistic or anxious thoughts and not encouraging avoidance
questions.explanation: Supporters are taught to help challenge anxious thoughts and to avoid accommodating avoidance, because avoidance maintains the phobia. Shielding the person from the stimulus may seem kind but reinforces the fear.

questions.stem: Lucas's mother always checks each room for spiders and removes them before he goes in. According to psychoeducation for supporters, why is this unhelpful?
options: It increases GABA activity in Lucas's brain, which strengthens the conditioned response
It pairs relaxation with fear on his hierarchy, which undoes systematic desensitisation
It supports avoidance, which negatively reinforces his fear and stops him learning he can cope
It exposes Lucas to the phobic stimulus far too quickly, before he has learned to relax
questions.explanation: By removing spiders for him, his mother helps Lucas avoid the stimulus, so his anxiety is relieved and avoidance is negatively reinforced. Psychoeducation teaches supporters not to encourage avoidance behaviours.

questions.stem: Why is a biopsychosocial approach used to treat specific phobia?
options: Phobia arises from interacting biological, psychological and social factors, so combined interventions target more causes
Each phobia has only one cause, so a single intervention chosen from the most relevant domain is always going to be enough
Biological treatments are always ineffective for phobia, so psychological and social treatments replace them
It means using medication from each domain, with no need for therapy or support from family and friends
questions.explanation: Because several kinds of factors contribute to phobia, interventions that address biological symptoms, thoughts and behaviours, and social support together are more likely to be effective. Benzodiazepines can be useful for short-term management, so biological treatments are not always ineffective.

questions.stem: Which is a biological protective factor for mental wellbeing?
options: Adequate sleep
Mindfulness meditation
Support from friends
Cognitive behavioural strategies
questions.explanation: In the biopsychosocial approach, adequate sleep, nutrition and hydration are biological protective factors. Mindfulness and cognitive behavioural strategies are psychological, and support from friends is social.

questions.stem: Mindfulness meditation supports mental wellbeing by:
options: suppressing all thoughts and emotions until the mind is completely blank
analysing past mistakes in detail to work out who was at fault
planning a response in advance for every problem that might arise
training attention on the present moment in a non-judgemental way
questions.explanation: Mindfulness meditation involves deliberately paying attention to the present, noticing thoughts and feelings without judging them. It does not aim to suppress all thoughts.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of social support that is authentic and energising?
options: A friend who listens genuinely and leaves you feeling uplifted after you talk
Hundreds of online followers who rarely interact with you or what you post
A relative who offers help but criticises you each time you accept it
A group you keep attending only because you feel obliged to be there
questions.explanation: Authentic support is genuine, and energising support leaves a person feeling better rather than drained. Large online followings or obligation-based contact do not provide that kind of support.

questions.stem: Why is adequate hydration considered a protective factor for mental wellbeing?
options: Water contains melatonin, so drinking more improves the timing of the sleep-wake cycle
Hydration increases the activity of glutamate, which reduces feelings of anxiety
Drinking more water removes the body's need for sleep and adequate nutrition
Even mild dehydration can impair mood, concentration and other cognitive functioning
questions.explanation: Research shows that even mild dehydration can lower mood and impair attention and memory, so staying hydrated helps maintain wellbeing. Water does not contain melatonin, and hydration does not replace sleep or nutrition.

questions.stem: How does adequate nutritional intake help to maintain mental wellbeing?
options: A balanced diet removes the need for sleep, because nutrients restore the brain during the day
Nutrition affects physical health only, so any of its benefits for wellbeing come from changes in weight alone
A diet high in sugar raises serotonin permanently, protecting a person against mental disorders
A balanced diet supplies the nutrients needed for brain function and supports healthy gut microbiota
questions.explanation: The brain needs a range of nutrients to function and to produce neurotransmitters, and diet shapes the gut microbiota that communicate with the brain through the gut–brain axis. Nutrition does not replace sleep, and its benefits are not limited to physical health.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a cognitive behavioural strategy for maintaining mental wellbeing?
options: Focusing on the sensation of breathing and letting thoughts pass without judging them
Eating regular, balanced meals and drinking enough water throughout the day
Spending time with friends who are supportive and leave you feeling energised
Noticing the thought 'I always fail' and replacing it with 'I pass most tests when I prepare'
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural strategies identify unhelpful thoughts and replace them with more realistic ones. Focusing on the breath without judgement is mindfulness meditation, a different psychological protective factor.

questions.stem: Daniel's family regularly share meals and encourage him, and he volunteers at a local sports club. In a biopsychosocial approach, these are:
options: social risk factors
social protective factors
psychological protective factors
biological protective factors
questions.explanation: Support from family, friends and community is a social protective factor. Psychological protective factors include mindfulness and cognitive behavioural strategies.

questions.stem: Sienna sleeps about nine hours a night, practises mindfulness daily and has a close group of supportive friends. Which statement best explains the benefit of this combination?
options: Protective factors across biological, psychological and social domains interact to support her wellbeing
Only her sleep is important, because biological factors alone determine a person's wellbeing
These protective factors will prevent her from ever experiencing any stress or anxiety at any point in future
These are risk factors that will make her more vulnerable to developing a specific phobia
questions.explanation: A biopsychosocial approach views protective factors as working together, so strengths in all three domains give the best support for maintaining wellbeing. Protective factors reduce the impact of stressors but do not stop a person ever experiencing stress.
